name: GFPT1-related congenital myasthenic syndrome (limb-girdle CMS with tubular aggregates)

clinicalPearls: GFPT1 encodes the rate-limiting enzyme of the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway, glutamine-fructose-6-phosphate transaminase 1, which supplies substrate for protein N- and O-glycosylation.
This is the prototypical glycosylation-defect congenital myasthenic syndrome and characteristically produces a limb-girdle pattern of fatigable weakness with relative sparing of ocular muscles.
Onset is often in childhood rather than the neonatal period, with proximal shoulder- and hip-girdle weakness that can be mistaken for a limb-girdle muscular dystrophy or an inflammatory myopathy.
Muscle biopsy classically shows tubular aggregates, a helpful but not universal or specific histological clue.
Creatine kinase may be mildly to moderately raised, further blurring the distinction from a primary myopathy.
Anticholinesterase medication such as pyridostigmine is often beneficial in this subtype, and salbutamol/albuterol or 3,4-diaminopyridine may be used as adjuncts.
The decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation confirms the neuromuscular junction basis and directs genetic testing toward the glycosylation-pathway genes.
reference.pathophysiology: GFPT1-related congenital myasthenic syndrome is caused by biallelic variants in GFPT1, which encodes glutamine-fructose-6-phosphate transaminase 1, the rate-limiting and controlling enzyme of the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway. This pathway generates uridine diphosphate N-acetylglucosamine, the essential donor substrate for both N-linked and O-linked glycosylation of proteins. Reduced GFPT1 activity limits the supply of these glycosylation precursors, impairing the correct glycosylation, assembly, trafficking and stability of glycoproteins critical to the neuromuscular junction, including the acetylcholine receptor and endplate structural components. The consequence is a poorly developed and structurally simplified postsynaptic apparatus with reduced acetylcholine receptor expression and, in many patients, secondary myopathic change with formation of tubular aggregates within muscle fibres. The reduced density and impaired function of endplate glycoproteins lowers the safety margin of neuromuscular transmission, producing predominantly proximal, limb-girdle fatigable weakness. Because acetylcholine receptor availability is reduced but acetylcholinesterase function is intact, measures that prolong or amplify acetylcholine action at the endplate, such as anticholinesterases, are frequently helpful.
additionalDifferentials: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophies given the proximal weakness and raised creatine kinase
Other glycosylation-pathway congenital myasthenic syndromes including DPAGT1 and ALG2/ALG14 subtypes, which also cause limb-girdle CMS with tubular aggregates
Autoimmune myasthenia gravis with limb-girdle presentation
Metabolic and mitochondrial myopathies presenting with proximal fatigable weakness
additionalInvestigations: Repetitive nerve stimulation demonstrating a decremental response
Single-fibre electromyography showing increased jitter and blocking
GFPT1 sequencing within a congenital myasthenic syndrome gene panel, with attention to the wider glycosylation-pathway genes
Muscle biopsy looking for tubular aggregates and to help exclude a primary myopathy
Acetylcholine receptor and MuSK antibody testing to exclude autoimmune myasthenia
redFlags: Development of respiratory muscle weakness or nocturnal hypoventilation
Rapidly progressive proximal weakness raising concern for an alternative diagnosis
Bulbar symptoms with swallowing difficulty and aspiration risk
Loss of independent ambulation indicating significant functional decline
reference.prognosis: Many patients respond well to anticholinesterase therapy and maintain good long-term function, though the limb-girdle weakness can be progressive in some and a minority develop respiratory involvement. Early recognition allows effective treatment and avoids inappropriate immunotherapy for a presumed myopathy.
pitfalls: Diagnosing a limb-girdle muscular dystrophy or inflammatory myopathy on the basis of proximal weakness and raised creatine kinase, and missing the treatable neuromuscular junction disorder.
Assuming ocular involvement must be present; its relative absence is characteristic and should not exclude the diagnosis.
Treating with immunosuppression for presumed inflammatory myopathy rather than recognising a genetic congenital myasthenic syndrome.
Regarding tubular aggregates as diagnostic; they support but do not confirm the subtype and may be absent.
